_comment: Conformance cases for evaluate_condition, taken from datrail/gateway's gateway-core/tests/vectors/v2/decide.json at 6758b77; its whole-bundle cases are the walk's. A ticket is the payload as the gateway's case gives it, or null without a usable ticket. Headers are the lines as sent. Endpoint keys are slugless, as the gateway reads them; a case marked `retargeted` moves a key that isn't one onto one that is, as the field says. A case marked `differs` is answered otherwise by the gateway: the three operands past what a double holds, which the contract compares as infinity and this reader refuses.

cases.name: uninterpretable — a field outside the table
cases.note: Rail Center can learn a field this enforcement point has not. The natural shape — a lookup defaulting to false — silently stops enforcing a block rule.

cases.name: uninterpretable — an operator outside the table
request.endpoint_key not_existing does not hold on a call naming a tool
cases.note: The key is a value in the request like any other: `not_existing` holds only where the call named no tool.

cases.name: request.endpoint_key existing holds on a call naming a tool
eq on a list does not hold when a value differs
cases.note: On a list, eq holds only when every value equals the operand; this list's one value is not "x".

cases.name: in on a list does not hold when no value is a member
matches reads any string claim
cases.note: No operator is tied to a field: a glob over a ticket claim is the policy's to write.

cases.name: contains does not hold on a string claim
cases.note: `contains` asks a list; a string is not a one-element list of itself.

cases.name: matches does not hold on a number claim
uninterpretable — a string operand for an ordered operator
cases.note: Not a rule that is false — one that can never be true, which is the failure an operator is least likely to notice.

cases.name: uninterpretable — a list operand for an ordered operator
uninterpretable — a boolean operand for an ordered operator
cases.note: A boolean is not a number, here or in the reference.

cases.name: uninterpretable — a null operand for an ordered operator
uninterpretable — a non-scalar operand for eq
uninterpretable — a boolean operand for ne
uninterpretable — a null operand for eq
uninterpretable — a non-list operand for in
uninterpretable — a non-scalar operand for contains
uninterpretable — a non-string pattern for matches
cases.note: Refused at validation rather than treated as a pattern that never matches: the key is always a string, so a non-string pattern can never hold.

cases.name: uninterpretable — a condition that is not an object
uninterpretable — a condition that is a list
uninterpretable — a field that is not a string
uninterpretable — an operator that is not a string
uninterpretable — a field that is missing entirely
uninterpretable — an operator that is missing entirely
uninterpretable — an unknown field is refused even where no ticket was read
cases.note: The refusal is a property of the rule, not of what it would have resolved against. A reader that resolved first and refused second would answer differently here.

cases.name: ticket is not_existing for an absent ticket
cases.note: no header at all. All four unusable states fold into one answer: the `ticket` source exists only for a usable ticket.

cases.name: ticket is not_existing for an undecodable ticket
cases.note: a header that does not decode. All four unusable states fold into one answer: the `ticket` source exists only for a usable ticket.

cases.name: ticket is not_existing for an expired ticket
ticket is not_existing for a malformed ticket
cases.note: An `exp` that is not a number: the payload is readable and is not a ticket.

cases.name: ticket is existing for a valid ticket
ticket is not not_existing for a valid ticket
uninterpretable — a path with no source
cases.note: The first segment names the source; `ticket` and `request` are the only two.

cases.name: uninterpretable — a source this gateway does not build
uninterpretable — an empty path
uninterpretable — the retired field key
cases.note: `{field, operator}` is the retired shape: no `path`, so nothing can be read.

cases.name: request.headers — a header sent once is its value
request.headers — names are lowercased
cases.note: HTTP header names are case-insensitive; the path uses the lowercase name.

cases.name: request.headers — a path in another case reads nothing
request.headers — a repeated header is a list, so eq does not hold
request.headers — a repeated header satisfies contains
request.headers — an absent header is not_existing
request.headers — matches reads a header
request.headers — the x-rail header itself is a header
cases.note: Raw presence, whatever the ticket read as. Whether a usable ticket arrived is the `ticket` source's to say.

cases.name: eq on a list holds only when every value equals
eq on a list of one repeated value holds
ne on a list holds when any value differs
cases.note: The reading that keeps an allowlist closed: a value beside the allowed one is a value that is not it.

cases.name: ne on a list does not hold when every value equals
eq and ne on an empty list hold for neither — eq
eq and ne on an empty list hold for neither — ne
ne on a list does not coerce its values
ne on a list counts a boolean value as differing
cases.note: On a list, a value that is not a scalar never equals the operand, so it is a value that differs; on a scalar claim the same boolean satisfies neither eq nor ne.

cases.name: ne on a list counts an object value as differing
eq on a list does not hold beside a boolean value
eq on a list does not hold beside an object value
not_contains holds when no value equals
not_contains does not hold when a value equals
not_contains holds on an empty list
not_contains does not hold on an absent value
cases.note: It declines where contains does, rather than holding as a negation would.

cases.name: not_contains does not hold on a string claim
uninterpretable — not_contains needs a scalar operand
not_contains takes a number operand — holds when no value equals
cases.note: A number is a scalar operand, as for contains; refusing it would answer every request reaching the rule with an error.

cases.name: not_contains takes a number operand — does not hold when a value equals
request.headers — a comma-separated value is a list
cases.note: Values are split on commas, whitespace trimmed, so one line carrying two values reads as two lines do — on every host.

cases.name: request.headers — a bare comma splits as a spaced one does
cases.note: The split is on the comma, not on a comma and a space, so dropping the space does not keep the line one value.

cases.name: request.headers — every value equals across a bare comma
request.headers — a comma-separated value does not satisfy eq on the whole
request.headers — lines and commas pool in order
request.headers — the allowlist denies a repeated foreign value
request.headers — the allowlist denies a foreign value beside the allowed one
request.headers — the allowlist admits the allowed value repeated
request.headers — not_contains reads a header
in on an empty list holds for nothing
in on a list: a non-scalar value is a member of nothing
matches on a list holds when any value matches
matches on a list does not hold when no value matches
matches on a list: a value that is not a string never matches
matches on an empty list holds for nothing
request.headers — a denylist matches a value beside another
cases.note: matches holds when any value does, so a wildcard denylist is one rule however the header splits.

cases.name: request.headers — a User-Agent split by its own comma still matches
headers: Mozilla/5.0 (X11; Linux x86_64) AppleWebKit/537.36 (KHTML, like Gecko) Chrome/129.0 Safari/537.36

cases.name: request.headers — in holds when any value is listed
an expired ticket's score does not outlive it
cases.note: The claims are still readable as text and are not a basis for any decision. This is the case that rule exists for.

cases.name: an expired ticket's claims are absent rather than retained
a claim whose key is absent from the payload resolves to absent
cases.note: The one an implementation forgets: reading claims[field] and testing === null leaves an omitted key reading as present. Deleting a key from an unsigned ticket is free.

cases.name: a claim that is present and null resolves to absent
cases.note: A null is how a mint says it has no value, and a rule meaning 'deny an agent with no score' has to catch it by the same door as an omitted key.

cases.name: a claim that is present and null is not present
a claim of zero is present
cases.note: The likely drift: testing the value's truth rather than its presence treats all three as missing.

cases.name: a claim of zero is not missing
a claim of an empty string is present
cases.note: The likely drift: testing the value's truth rather than its presence treats all three as missing.

cases.name: a claim of an empty string is not missing
a flat posture_score is read like any other key
cases.note: The gateway knows no claim names, so `ticket.posture_score` reads whatever the ticket carries there; Rail Center refuses to publish a path its ticket does not have.

cases.name: uninterpretable — tier is no longer a field
uninterpretable — scored_at is no longer a field
a category score is read by its path
an object is existing
cases.note: A path may end on an object; existing and not_existing read it like any value.

cases.name: an object path is not not_existing when present
uninterpretable — the ticket's own id is not a field
cases.note: `id` travels into a denial as `ticket_id`; it is not a claim a policy asks about.

cases.name: a top-level object is existing
alignment is not not_existing when present
an ordered op against a string claim does not hold
contains does not hold on a string claim — the baseline id
eq on a list does not hold when a value differs — drifted
in on a list holds when any value is a member
cases.note: On a list, in holds when any value is in the operand.

cases.name: posture.overall.score — present holds on a full ticket
posture.overall.score — eq holds on the nested value
posture.overall.score — ne holds against a different value
posture.overall.score — in holds for a member
posture.overall.score — gte holds above the bound
posture.overall.level — eq holds on the band
posture.overall.level — in holds for one of several bands
posture.overall.level — ne holds for another band
posture.overall.level — an operand outside the four bands is read, and does not hold
cases.note: The operand is not checked against the bands, as `sandbox_type`'s is not: a rule naming a band that does not exist is one that never fires, not one that is refused.

cases.name: posture.overall.level — missing holds when the overall object carries only a score
alignment.baseline.id — present holds when the agent has a baseline
alignment.baseline.id — eq holds on the baseline's id
alignment.baseline.id — ne holds against another id
alignment.baseline.id — in holds for a member
alignment.baseline.id — missing holds when the agent has no baseline
cases.note: `alignment.baseline` is absent when there is none, so the id below it is a missing intermediate's child, and `missing` holds.

cases.name: alignment.baseline.id — ne does not hold when the agent has no baseline
cases.note: `ne` never holds for an absent claim, however it came to be absent. 'No baseline, or a different one' is two conditions.

cases.name: alignment.baseline.label — eq holds on the label
alignment.baseline.label — eq compares exactly, with no case folding
alignment.baseline.label — ne holds against another label
alignment.baseline.label — in holds for a member
alignment.baseline.label — present holds when the agent has a baseline
alignment.baseline.label — missing holds when the agent has no baseline
alignment.baseline.label — a null baseline is no baseline
alignment.drifted — contains holds for a drifted attribute
alignment.drifted — contains does not hold for one that did not drift
alignment.drifted — contains does not substring-match a string claim
cases.note: A string is not a one-element list of itself.

cases.name: alignment.drifted — an empty list is present
cases.note: Nothing drifted is a claim, not the absence of one.

cases.name: alignment.drifted — an empty list is not missing
alignment.drifted — missing holds when alignment is absent
a missing intermediate — no posture object at all
cases.note: A ticket with nothing on the way to a claim has no claim. Deleting a whole object from an unsigned ticket is as free as deleting a key.

cases.name: a missing intermediate — posture with no overall
a missing intermediate — an empty posture object
a missing intermediate — a null on the way is absent
a missing intermediate — a number on the way is absent, not an error
cases.note: An intermediate that is not an object has no keys. Raising here would let a ticket's sender choose a 503.

cases.name: a list on the way is absent, even one holding the next key
cases.note: A path steps through objects only. Reading through a list would give an index or a membership test a meaning the contract never gave it, and a reader that tries raises here instead: a ticket's sender then decides whether the chain is walked.

cases.name: a string on the way is absent, even one containing the next key
cases.note: The same for a string, where `in` is a substring test and indexing by a key raises.

cases.name: a missing intermediate — a list on the way is absent
cases.note: No segment is a list index.

cases.name: a missing intermediate — a string on the way is absent
a missing intermediate is not present
an ordered operator does not hold across a missing intermediate
cases.note: Which is why a rule meaning 'deny a low or missing score' is two policies.

cases.name: a missing intermediate does not satisfy contains
a dotted top-level key is not the nested claim
cases.note: The field is a path walked one key at a time, never a key looked up whole.

cases.name: a dotted top-level key does not satisfy an ordered rule
an expired ticket's nested claims are absent too
a claim of an empty list is present
cases.note: The likely drift: testing the value's truth rather than its presence treats all three as missing.

cases.name: a claim of an empty list is not missing
endpoint_key resolves to the key the decision was given
agent_id — present holds on the claim
cases.note: The table carries eleven fields, and this group pins the five that are read straight off the claims. A field the table stops carrying is not a condition that fails to hold: it refuses the request, so a rule Rail Center published against it answers 503 here on every request whose walk reaches it and decides normally there.

cases.name: agent_id — missing holds where no usable ticket was read
cases.note: A ticket is not valid without a string agent_id, so this claim is absent only where the ticket itself is unusable — which is the one way the field can answer missing at all.

cases.name: agent_id — eq holds against the claim
agent_id — ne holds against a different value
agent_id — in holds for a member
sandbox_id — present holds on the claim
sandbox_id — missing holds where the payload omits the key
cases.note: Reading a ticket turns on agent_id and exp alone, so a payload without this claim is a valid ticket carrying an absent claim rather than an unreadable one. The ticket is unsigned: deleting a key is free, and a rule keying on this field has to survive it.

cases.name: sandbox_id — eq holds against the claim
sandbox_id — ne holds against a different value
sandbox_id — in holds for a member
sandbox_type — present holds on the claim
sandbox_type — missing holds where the payload omits the key
sandbox_type — eq holds against the claim
sandbox_type — ne holds against a different value
sandbox_type — in holds for a member
environment_fingerprint — present holds on the claim
environment_fingerprint — missing holds where the payload omits the key
environment_fingerprint — eq holds against the claim
environment_fingerprint — ne holds against a different value
environment_fingerprint — in holds for a member
eq compares a string to a string
a string never equals a number
cases.note: "40" does not satisfy eq 40. JavaScript's == and Number() both coerce and must not be used.

cases.name: an empty string never equals zero
a boolean claim never equals one
cases.note: True == 1 in Python and true === 1 is false in TypeScript, so a reader that does not exclude booleans makes a rule's meaning depend on which language read it.

cases.name: a boolean claim never equals zero
eq on a one-value list holds when that value equals
cases.note: On a list, eq holds when every value equals the operand.

cases.name: a string score is catchable by eq against the same string
cases.note: An allow-list of forgeries rather than a type check, and the difference between 'hard to express' and 'not expressible'.

cases.name: and does not hold against a numeric claim of the same value
ne holds for a different scalar
ne does not hold for an absent field
cases.note: A rule meaning 'absent or different' is two conditions.

cases.name: a boolean claim does not satisfy ne
cases.note: Not comparing is not the same as comparing unequal.

cases.name: ne on a list holds when a value differs
cases.note: On a list, ne holds when any value differs from the operand: a forged one-value list is read value by value, not refused as a kind.

cases.name: an object claim does not satisfy ne
lt compares two numbers
a numeric string does not satisfy lt
cases.note: It is not a number at all. The ordered operators must check the type before comparing rather than convert.

cases.name: a boolean claim does not satisfy lt
a list claim does not satisfy lt
lte holds at the bound
lt does not hold at the bound
gte holds at the bound
gt holds above it
a float claim compares against a whole operand
two integers a double cannot separate are equal
cases.note: 2**53 and 2**53 + 1 are distinct integers in an arbitrary-precision language and the same double in JavaScript. Every number reaching a comparison is narrowed, on both sides of it.

cases.name: and neither is less than the other
cases.note: The other half. Narrowing only the claim leaves the divergence on the operand.

cases.name: an integer past the double range saturates rather than raising
cases.differs: the gateway compares it as infinity; this reader refuses it, as rail-center/task.md proposes Rail Center do on publish; its ticket, scored past a double too, is undecodable here, so none is usable
cases.note: Both saturate to the same infinity and compare equal. float() raises where JavaScript saturates, and an exception where a comparison belongs is neither an allow nor a deny.

cases.name: and so does one past the negative end
cases.differs: the gateway compares it as infinity; this reader refuses it, as rail-center/task.md proposes Rail Center do on publish; its ticket, scored past a double too, is undecodable here, so none is usable

cases.name: an operand overflowing to infinity is compared, not refused
cases.differs: the gateway compares it as infinity; this reader refuses it, as rail-center/task.md proposes Rail Center do on publish

cases.name: in holds for a member
in does not coerce its elements
in holds for a numeric member
in on a one-value list holds for that value
a non-scalar element of an in operand never matches
cases.note: Accepted by validation and simply never matches, so no comparison ever sees two containers.

cases.name: a boolean element of an in operand never matches a boolean claim
contains holds when the list carries the operand
contains does not substring-match a string claim
cases.note: A reader reaching for `operand in claim` would satisfy a rule about delivery.admin with a skills of delivery.administrator.

cases.name: contains does not substring-match an element either
contains requires the claim to be a list
a boolean element of a list claim does not satisfy contains
matches — a trailing star covers a whole segment
matches — a star spans the segment separator
cases.note: `*` includes the `.` that separates endpoint-key segments.

cases.name: matches — a star stands for an empty run
cases.retargeted: a star after a non-empty call

cases.name: matches — a pattern is anchored at the start
cases.note: A pattern matching anywhere within the key would be a different rule from the one an operator reads it as.

cases.name: matches — a leading star covers everything before the suffix
matches — a pattern is anchored at the end
matches — a bare star matches any key
matches — a pattern carrying no star is a literal
cases.note: It matches exactly what `eq` would. Accepted rather than refused, because refusing it would mean broadening a rule from `delivery.orders` to `delivery.*` had to change the operator too.

cases.name: matches — a literal is not a prefix rule
cases.note: A reader answering `key.startswith(pattern)` on the starless branch widens every literal pattern an operator wrote.

cases.name: matches — a literal does not match a longer key
matches — the two ends may abut
cases.note: Pinned from both sides, because startswith-and-endswith is the natural shape to write.

cases.name: matches — the two ends must not overlap
cases.note: `ab*ab` does not match `ab`, though the key both starts and ends with `ab`. `*` stands for a run of characters, possibly empty, but never for characters counted twice.

cases.name: matches — the two ends with a run between them
matches — a key too short for both ends
matches — an interior segment must fit before the suffix
cases.note: A reader that checks only that the segment was found lets it match the suffix's own characters a second time.

cases.name: matches — and does fit where the key carries it twice
matches — an interior segment matched at its earliest position
cases.note: With `*` the only metacharacter every interior segment is a fixed literal, so taking one early never rules out a match a fuller search would find — which is why no backtracking is needed to be correct.

cases.name: matches — two stars are one
matches — two stars are one, over a run
matches — an embedded newline is an ordinary character in a pattern
matches — a star matches a newline
cases.note: `.` does not without re.DOTALL in Python or the `s` flag in JavaScript, so the default regex translation of `*` to `.*` refuses a key this accepts.

cases.name: matches — a literal does not match a key with a trailing newline
cases.note: Python's `$` matches immediately before a trailing newline, so a `^…$` translation accepts a key this rule does not name. The two newline rules pull in opposite directions and a translation can get either wrong alone.

cases.name: matches — no case folding, on the key
cases.note: `FinRetail.*` matches nothing that `finretail.*` matches. Folding would reintroduce the divergence in the form nobody writes a test for, because the locale-sensitive way to fold sits a keystroke from the locale-independent one.

cases.name: matches — no case folding, on the pattern
matches — no Unicode normalisation
cases.note: `é` and `e` plus a combining acute (`́`) are canonically equivalent and are not the same key here. Normalising both sides to NFC is a habit picked up from path handling, and it makes the set of keys a rule covers depend on which form the operator's editor saved.

cases.name: matches — the same form matches itself
cases.note: So the case above is a statement about normalisation rather than about the pattern being wrong.

cases.name: matches — a question mark is a literal
cases.note: Every character but `*` is a literal — `?`, `[`, `]` and `\` included — and there is no escape character.

cases.name: matches — a question mark matches itself
matches — a bracket expression is not a character class
cases.note: Python's fnmatch supports `[seq]` and `[!seq]` and folds case on some platforms, which is why it must not be used.

cases.name: matches — a bracket expression matches itself
matches — a backslash is a literal
matches — a backslash does not escape a star
cases.note: There being no escape character means a literal `*` cannot be written; an endpoint key containing one is matched by `eq`.
